detailed_summary: This paper addresses two long-standing regularizations in quantum information theory: the classical capacity of a noisy quantum channel and its entanglement cost. The authors prove that for every qubit-to-qubit channel that admits a pure output state, both the Holevo information and the entanglement of formation are additive with respect to any finite-dimensional partner channel. This implies that the unassisted classical capacity equals the single-use Holevo information, and the parallel entanglement cost equals the single-use entanglement of formation. The result covers all qubit-to-qubit channels of Kraus rank at most two, a broad class that includes the amplitude damping channel. For the amplitude damping channel with damping probability p, the authors show that the classical capacity is attained by a binary pure-state ensemble with collective decoding, and the entanglement cost is h_2((1+√p)/2) ebits per use. The central technical tool is a support criterion for strong superadditivity of entanglement of formation: if one marginal of a bipartite state has no support on the subspace where both local systems are orthogonal to fixed distinguished vectors, then strong superadditivity holds. This criterion is proven in arbitrary finite dimensions using a triangular block-matrix entropy inequality and decompositions that preserve two expectations. For amplitude damping, the authors also derive an exact finite-block Holevo deficit, identify the unique optimal average input for p<1, and construct a binary Kraus representation that attains the uniform formation bound.
key_contributions: Proves additivity of Holevo information and entanglement of formation for all qubit-to-qubit channels with a pure output, eliminating regularization for both classical capacity and entanglement cost.
Establishes a general support criterion for strong superadditivity of entanglement of formation in arbitrary finite dimensions, based on a triangular block-matrix entropy inequality.
Shows that for the amplitude damping channel, the unassisted classical capacity equals the single-use Holevo information, achieved by a binary pure-state ensemble with collective decoding.
Computes the exact entanglement cost of the amplitude damping channel as h_2((1+√p)/2) ebits per use, and identifies the unique optimal average input for p<1.
Derives an exact finite-block Holevo deficit for amplitude damping and constructs a binary Kraus representation attaining the uniform formation bound.
methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of quantum information-theoretic techniques and matrix analysis. The core methodological innovation is a support criterion for strong superadditivity of entanglement of formation, which is proven using a triangular block-matrix entropy inequality and decompositions that preserve two expectations. This criterion is then applied to qubit-to-qubit channels with a pure output to establish additivity of Holevo information and entanglement of formation. For the amplitude damping channel, the authors use explicit calculations to determine the optimal input ensemble and the exact entanglement cost, leveraging the binary Kraus representation and collective decoding. The proofs are rigorous and general, extending beyond the specific channel examples to arbitrary finite dimensions for the support criterion.
results_analysis: The main results are twofold: (1) For any qubit-to-qubit channel with a pure output, the Holevo information and entanglement of formation are additive with any finite-dimensional partner channel, implying that the classical capacity and entanglement cost require no regularization. (2) For the amplitude damping channel with damping probability p, the classical capacity is exactly the single-use Holevo information, achieved by a binary pure-state ensemble with collective decoding, and the entanglement cost is h_2((1+√p)/2) ebits per use. The paper also provides an exact finite-block Holevo deficit and identifies the unique optimal average input for p<1. These results are significant because they resolve regularizations for a broad class of channels and provide explicit formulas for a practically relevant channel.
strengths: The paper resolves two major regularizations (classical capacity and entanglement cost) for a wide class of qubit-to-qubit channels, which is a significant theoretical advance.
The support criterion for strong superadditivity of entanglement of formation is proven in arbitrary finite dimensions, making it a powerful and general tool.
The results for the amplitude damping channel are explicit and exact, including the entanglement cost and the optimal input ensemble, which are valuable for practical applications.
The methodology combines rigorous mathematical proofs with concrete channel analysis, demonstrating both depth and applicability.
limitations: The additivity results are restricted to qubit-to-qubit channels that admit a pure output, which, while broad, do not cover all quantum channels.
The paper does not address the computational complexity of finding the optimal input ensemble for general channels, though it does for amplitude damping.
The support criterion, while general, may be difficult to verify for arbitrary states, limiting its immediate applicability to other channels.
connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly quantum information theory and quantum communication. It addresses fundamental questions about the capacity of noisy quantum channels and the entanglement required for communication, which are central to understanding quantum information processing. The results on amplitude damping, a common noise model in quantum computing and communication, have practical implications for error correction and channel coding. The support criterion for strong superadditivity of entanglement of formation also connects to broader studies of entanglement theory and quantum correlations.
overall_assessment: This paper makes a substantial contribution to quantum information theory by eliminating regularizations for a significant class of qubit-to-qubit channels. The proof of the support criterion for strong superadditivity of entanglement of formation is a notable technical achievement, and the explicit results for the amplitude damping channel are both elegant and useful. The work is rigorous, well-structured, and likely to inspire further research on additivity properties of other channels. Its significance lies in providing exact, computable formulas for channel capacities and entanglement costs, which are essential for both theoretical understanding and practical quantum communication.
